newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle astronauts begin Hubble upgrade.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle astronauts begin Hubble upgrade.

text.p: Two spacewalking astronauts from shuttle Discovery eased two new scientific instruments into the Hubble Space Telescope on Friday, starting a four-day $350 million orbital tune-up.
Mark Lee and Steve Smith gently removed two of the telescope's ageing instruments and replaced them with an improved light-splitting spectrograph and a multipurpose infrared camera.

It was an eventful night for the shuttle crew and ground controllers at mission control in Houston. The start of the spacewalk was delayed when one of the telescope's solar arrays was put in a spin and there were problems closing a set of doors, but all of the work was accomplished.
The astronauts returned to Discovery's airlock after 6-1/2 hours outside, slightly longer than planned.
"I'm sorry we made this a little bit more exciting than we had in mind, but we feel like everything turned out pretty good," Discovery astronaut Joe Tanner said.

"It is almost impossible to imagine the Hubble Space Telescope being any better than it has been for the last three years, but you guys have made it so," mission control's Jeff Hoffman radioed the crew.
The first task for the astronauts was the installation of a $125 million state-of-the-art-spectrograph, called STIS, which will aid astronomers seeking massive black holes.
It proved a little tricky to fit the 700 lb (320 kg), refrigerator-sized spectrograph precisely inside the telescope, but the work was completed on time.
An initial test of the instrument showed it was working properly, and the astronauts turned their attention toward installing the $105 million NICMOS infrared camera.

The instrument's detectors, cooled to -355 degrees Fahrenheit (-215 Celsius) by a block of frozen nitrogen, will allow astronomers to see deeper into the universe and peer through veils of dust to see newborn stars. Scientists hoped the instrument would also take the first images of planets orbiting distant stars.
The astronauts struggled to close a pair of access doors to the telescope's instrument bay. They were forced to turn up the power on their bolt-turning tool in order to latch the doors properly.
Lee and Smith, wearing bulky white spacesuits, began the spacewalk at about 11:45 p.m. EST on Thursday (0445 GMT Friday) as the shuttle soared 360 miles (575 km) above Australia.
"Oh my gosh, beautiful," said Smith as he floated outside with the gleaming, silver observatory towering overhead. "Wow, look at that telescope," added Lee.
Smith worked perched on the end of the shuttle's 50-ft (15 metre) robot arm, while Lee floated free, often completely inside the telescope.
The start of the spacewalk was held up for one hour and 45 minutes after one of the telescope's two fragile solar arrays swung round violently and unexpectedly.

"We saw something real unusual," Tanner radioed mission control. "The ... array skewed from horizontal to vertical and then about halfway back to horizontal." The rapid movement of the 40-ft (12-metre)-long panel occurred in just five seconds, he said.
"That must have been very dramatic," Hoffman replied.

Lee and Smith were about to leave the shuttle's airlock when the incident occurred. Flight controllers said air vented into space from the airlock compartment had struck the panel and set it moving. The delicate array appeared undamaged by the incident, they said.

Three more spacewalks were planned to complete the refurbishment of the telescope. Other upgrades included the installation of a new digital tape recorder, a more accurate guidance sensor for pointing the telescope and various improved electronic boxes.
It was the first time astronauts had worked on the $2 billion orbiting observatory since the 1993 repair that fixed its blurred vision.
